blocks.title: Hobbies
paragraphs: A hobby is something you do for enjoyment, not for work. People choose hobbies for many different reasons, and there are many different kinds. In this material, you will read about why hobbies matter, how they help you grow, and how to start one that fits your life.

items.prompt: Do you have a hobby right now? What is it?
items.answer: Any honest answer is good. For example: "Yes, I like drawing. I do it on weekends."

items.prompt: Think of one thing you enjoy doing in your free time. Is it something you do alone or with other people?
items.answer: Any honest answer is good. For example: "I usually read books alone at home."

items.prompt: If you could try any new hobby today, what would it be? Why?
items.answer: Any honest answer is good. For example: "I would like to try cooking because I enjoy eating new foods."

blocks.title: Part 1: Why People Choose Hobbies
paragraphs: People choose hobbies for many reasons. Some want to relax after a busy day at work or school. Others want to feel creative. For example, Mia started painting because her job was very stressful. She says painting helps her feel calm. Some people choose hobbies because they want to learn something new. For example, Carlos started learning to cook when he moved to a new city. He wanted to make the food he missed from home. A hobby gives you time to do something you enjoy, just for yourself.

images.alt: A map artist draws at a desk while three friends wave from a text-free video call.

items.prompt: Why did Carlos start learning to cook?
items.answer: Carlos started learning to cook when he moved to a new city. He wanted to make the food he missed from home.
items.explanation:
The text says he moved to a new city and wanted to make familiar food.

Can you think of a time when a big change in your life made you want to start something new?

blocks.title: Part 2: Social and Solo Hobbies
paragraphs: Some hobbies are solo — you do them alone. Reading, journaling, and gardening are common solo hobbies. They are quiet and personal. Other hobbies are social — you do them with other people. Team sports, board game clubs, and choir groups are social hobbies. For example, Priya joined a local running club. She says she enjoys the exercise, but she also likes talking to people after the run. Both types have value. Solo hobbies give you quiet time to think. Social hobbies help you connect with others and feel less alone.

items.prompt: What does Priya enjoy about her running club?
items.answer: Priya enjoys the exercise and also likes talking to other people after the run.
items.explanation:
The text says she joined for exercise but also values the social time after running.

Do you prefer solo hobbies or social hobbies? Why?

blocks.title: Part 3: Building Skills Through Hobbies
paragraphs: Many hobbies help you build real skills over time. When you practice, you get better — and that feels good. For example, Tom started playing the guitar as a hobby three years ago. At first, his fingers hurt and the sounds were not nice. Now he plays songs for his family. He did not plan to become a professional musician. He just kept practising because he enjoyed it. Some hobby skills are also useful in other parts of life. For example, someone who blogs as a hobby often becomes a better writer at work too.

images.alt: A teenager calmly practices guitar before dinner while a wordless wall clock marks the early evening.

items.prompt: How did Tom's guitar playing change over three years?
items.answer: At first it was difficult and the sounds were not nice. After three years of practice, he can play songs for his family.
items.explanation:
The text describes his progress from struggling beginner to someone who plays for others.

Can you think of a skill you improved because you enjoyed practising it?

blocks.title: Part 4: Managing Time and Cost
paragraphs: Two common problems with hobbies are time and money. Many people say they want a hobby but feel too busy. A useful idea is to start small. Even fifteen or twenty minutes a few times a week is enough to begin. For example, Yuki wanted to learn watercolour painting but only had short breaks in her day. She started with ten-minute sketches and slowly built up. Some hobbies also cost money — equipment, lessons, or materials. But not all hobbies are expensive. Walking, writing, and learning a language with free apps cost very little. The key is to match the hobby to your real life, not an imaginary perfect schedule.

items.prompt: How did Yuki deal with not having much free time for her new hobby?
items.answer: She started with just ten-minute sketches during short breaks and slowly did more over time.
items.explanation:
The text says she matched her hobby to the small amount of time she actually had.

What is one low-cost hobby you could try in your own life right now?

blocks.title: Part 5: Trying Something New
paragraphs: Starting a new hobby can feel difficult. You might worry about being bad at it or looking silly. But everyone starts as a beginner. A good way to begin is to try one small step — watch a short video, borrow a book, or go to one introductory class. For example, Leo had never cooked before. He watched one online cooking video each weekend and tried the recipe the same day. After two months, he felt confident enough to cook for a friend. You do not need to be perfect to enjoy a hobby. The most important thing is that you find it interesting and keep going.

images.alt: Four watercolor panels show painting, swimming, collecting coins, and playing a board game together.

items.prompt: What small steps did Leo take to start his new cooking hobby?
items.answer: Leo watched one online cooking video each weekend and tried the recipe the same day. After two months, he felt confident enough to cook for a friend.
items.explanation:
The text shows he used a simple weekly routine to build his skills step by step.

What is one small first step you could take this week to try a hobby you are curious about?

items.prompt: Think about everything you read. Choose one hobby — real or imagined — and explain: Why does this hobby suit you? Is it social or solo? What skill could it help you build? How could you manage the time or cost?
items.answer: A good answer names a specific hobby and gives a reason for the choice. It says whether the hobby is social or solo, mentions one skill it could build, and suggests one practical way to manage time or cost. For example: "I would like to try photography. It is mostly a solo hobby, but I could join a photo walk group to make it more social. It would help me notice details and improve my eye for composition. I could start with my phone camera, so the cost is almost nothing, and practise for twenty minutes on weekend mornings."
items.explanation: This question asks you to connect the ideas from all five parts to your own life. There is no single correct answer.

rows.meaning: an activity you do regularly for enjoyment, not for work
rows.example: Gardening is a popular hobby for people who like being outdoors.
Reading is a solo hobby that you can enjoy anywhere.

rows.meaning: done with other people; involving company
rows.example: Joining a choir is a social hobby because you sing with a group.

rows.meaning: to do something regularly in order to improve
rows.example: She practises the piano for thirty minutes every evening.

rows.meaning: someone who is just starting to learn something
rows.example: Every expert was once a beginner.

rows.meaning: a plan that shows when you will do things
rows.example: He added painting to his weekly schedule on Saturday mornings.

rows.meaning: feeling sure about your ability to do something
rows.example: After two months of cooking, Leo felt confident enough to cook for a friend.

rows.meaning: the tools or objects you need for an activity
rows.example: Cycling requires some equipment, like a bicycle and a helmet.
